it, verify_academy.py rule 15 checks it, validate_claims.py scans every piece of
prose in it.
* a challenge stores IDs, never copies of scientific records: SID of an Atlas
study, node/edge id from pathway/model.json, lesson slug, guided-route id.
* every experiment result is either derived from a real study (evidence.sids)
or explicitly marked evidence.hypothetical -- the engine labels it on the page
and the gate refuses anything that is neither.
* result bars carry a qualitative level (none/low/mid/high), never a fabricated
number. They show direction and rank order as reported, and say so.

challenges.title: Is Rheb an ON/OFF switch?
challenges.subtitle: Nucleotide state, location, or both — and how you would tell
challenges.researchQuestion: Is Rheb-mediated regulation of mTORC1 determined mainly by nucleotide state, by localisation, or by both?

prerequisites.why: What the kinase integrates, and what its readouts are.
Why a claim about ‘mTOR’ is usually a claim about one of two complexes.
The GTP/GDP cycle, the TSC complex as a GAP, and the uncertainty this challenge starts from.

learningObjectives: Distinguish a claim about a protein's activation state from a claim about where that protein is
Rank candidate experiments by how well they separate two competing explanations
Identify what an overexpression result can and cannot support
Propose the control that would make a spatial claim interpretable

whatWeKnow.claim: TSC2 acts directly on Rheb's nucleotide cycle: it accelerates the conversion of Rheb-GTP to Rheb-GDP, and cells without a working TSC complex hold more Rheb-GTP and more mTOR signalling.
The loading step is under physiological control. Insulin raises Rheb-GTP in a PI3K-dependent way, and TSC1/TSC2 blocks that increase.
Raising Rheb is sufficient to raise mTORC1 output and cell growth in the systems where it was tested.

The amino-acid input works on position rather than on loading: the Rag GTPases bind raptor and move mTOR to a compartment that also holds Rheb, and a GTP-locked Rag mutant makes signalling resistant to amino-acid withdrawal.
The brake moves too. TSC2 accumulates on lysosomes whenever amino acids or growth factors are missing, so ‘state’ and ‘place’ are not two separate compartments of the problem.

uncertainty: Several of the foundational nucleotide-state experiments used overexpressed protein. They report what Rheb can do when there is more of it, which is a different statement from what endogenous Rheb does.
The two arms were largely measured in separate experiments, often in different cell types. Their relative contribution in one cell at one moment is not something the studies in this Atlas resolve.
No study in this corpus moves Rheb itself between compartments at endogenous levels while leaving its nucleotide cycle intact — which is the experiment the question is really asking for.

budget.note: Each step costs what its equipment costs. Running everything would take 160 units, and answering every sub-question that can be answered would take 120 — so this budget buys four of the six answers at most. Which four is the whole exercise.

lab.startNote: Three ways in: the cheap biochemical foundation, the physiological route, or straight at the question. None of them is wrong, and they do not cost the same.

goals.question: Is Rheb's nucleotide state actually controlled, and by what?
Does a physiological input move that control?
Can changing Rheb alone change the output?
goals.note: Two findings, and that is the point: an overexpression result only answers this once you have checked whether the input arm moved with it.

goals.question: Is where mTORC1 sits a control point in its own right?
Are state and place two separate variables at all?
Which arm contributes more, in one cell, at endogenous levels?
goals.note: Nothing in this corpus yields this. The only step that would address it returns a prediction rather than a result, so this sub-question stays open at any price — which is the honest ending of the challenge, not a gap in the menu.

nodes.label: In vitro GAP assay: does TSC2 unload Rheb directly?
nodes.equipment: Recombinant protein and a nucleotide-loading assay. No cells, no imaging — the cheapest thing on this menu, and it shows.
nodes.addresses: The nucleotide arm, and only its biochemistry

design.perturbation: Add the TSC2 GAP domain to Rheb preloaded with GTP
design.readout: Which nucleotide is bound to Rheb
design.control: Rheb without TSC2; a GAP-dead TSC2 mutant

result.caption: Direction and rank order as reported in the source study. The bars are a schematic of that direction, not measured values.

conclude: TSC2 acts on Rheb's nucleotide cycle itself, rather than somewhere further downstream.
The brake in the pathway diagram has a biochemical meaning: a GAP that speeds up unloading.
cannotConclude: Anything about where either protein sits — this is a tube, and it has no compartments.
Whether this rate is the one that matters at endogenous protein levels inside a cell.
nodes.informative: High for the mechanism of the brake, and zero for the question you actually asked: all four hypotheses predict this same result, so it cannot separate them. Spending 10 units here buys confidence in a step you were not doubting — though it is also what opens the two cell-based steps, so it is not money thrown away.

interpret.label: It supports my hypothesis
interpret.note: Be careful about what it supports. A result that every candidate explanation predicts does not favour any of them — it confirms shared background, which feels like progress and is not.

interpret.label: It weakens my hypothesis
interpret.note: It is hard to see how. No hypothesis on your list denies that TSC2 unloads Rheb; they differ about whether loading is what decides the output in a cell.

interpret.label: It is inconclusive for my question
interpret.note: That is the reading this result deserves. It is a clean, interpretable biochemical experiment about a step none of your hypotheses disputed.

interpret.label: It introduces an alternative explanation
interpret.note: Not really an alternative — more a reminder that the brake acts on the activator rather than on the kinase, which is worth keeping straight when you read the spatial experiments.

nodes.opensNote: Having the assay working is what makes the two cell-based steps worth doing at all.

falsify.prompt: Say it before you look: which of these results would weaken the model you are holding?

options.label: TSC2 leaves Rheb loaded — the brake acts somewhere else entirely
options.note: That would move the brake off Rheb and rearrange the diagram above it. It is the result that would cost you the most, which is exactly why it is worth naming before you look.

options.label: TSC2 unloads Rheb, the way the diagram says
options.note: This is the shared background every hypothesis on your list already predicts, so it cannot weaken any of them. Naming it as your falsifier is itself a signal that this step is not discriminating.

options.label: The effect appears only once there are cells involved
options.note: A tube has no compartments, so this design cannot show that either way. If it is what you care about, your units belong in the cell-based steps.

options.label: Nothing here would change my mind
options.note: Defensible for this step in particular, and worth saying aloud: if no outcome would move you, the ten units buy reassurance rather than information.

nodes.label: Does a physiological input change Rheb loading in cells?
nodes.equipment: Cell culture, serum starvation and stimulation, a GTP-loading pull-down and a western blot.
nodes.addresses: Whether the nucleotide arm is regulated at all

design.perturbation: Stimulate serum-starved cells with insulin, with and without co-expressed TSC1/TSC2
design.readout: Fraction of Rheb in the GTP state, alongside p-S6K1

result.caption: Direction and rank order as reported in the source study, which also places the insulin effect downstream of PI3K. Schematic, not measured values.

conclude: Rheb loading is a regulated variable in living cells, not a constant the cell sets once.
TSC1/TSC2 sits between the hormone and the loading step, which is what makes it the point where growth-factor signalling enters.
cannotConclude: That the loading change is what caused the p-S6K1 change — the two are measured together, and moving one without the other is a separate experiment.
Anything about position: nothing here reports where Rheb or mTORC1 were.
nodes.informative: Moderate. It separates ‘loading is regulated’ from ‘loading is constitutive’, which matters if you hold the localisation hypothesis in its strongest form. It is silent on the location arm.

interpret.label: It supports my hypothesis
interpret.note: If your hypothesis is nucleotide-dominant, this is real support for the premise — the arm is regulated. It is not yet support for the claim that this arm is the one that decides the output.

interpret.label: It weakens my hypothesis
interpret.note: Only for the strongest form of the localisation hypothesis, the one that treats loading as fixed background. The moderate form survives this result untouched.

interpret.label: It is inconclusive for my question
interpret.note: Defensible. Two things move together here, and the design does not break that pairing apart.

interpret.label: It introduces an alternative explanation
interpret.note: It does raise one: if insulin changes loading and output at once, some of the output change may come from elsewhere in the insulin arm rather than through Rheb.

nodes.opensNote: A regulated loading step is the reason to ask whether loading is what decides the output — and the reason to go looking at position.

falsify.prompt: Before the result: which outcome would weaken your working hypothesis?

options.label: Insulin leaves Rheb loading exactly where it was
options.note: That would take the nucleotide arm out of the regulated part of the pathway, and a nucleotide-dominant reading would lose its premise rather than just its scope.

options.label: Insulin raises loading, and the TSC complex blocks that rise
options.note: What the study reports. It supports the premise of the nucleotide arm without deciding whether that arm is the one that sets the output, so read it as a floor rather than a verdict.

options.label: Loading rises while p-S6K1 stays flat
options.note: That would split the two readouts and make loading look like a bystander. It would be the most interesting result on this card, and it is not the one that came out.

options.label: Nothing here would change my mind
options.note: Then the twenty units are buying a premise you already hold, and the question is whether the location arm can be bought instead.

nodes.label: Raise Rheb and see whether output follows
nodes.equipment: Cell culture and transfection or stable lines, western blot, plus Drosophila tissue for the growth readout.
nodes.addresses: Whether the nucleotide arm can drive the output on its own

design.perturbation: Overexpress Rheb, or a form biased toward the GTP state
design.readout: p-S6K1 and p-4E-BP1; cell and tissue growth
design.control: Empty vector; rapamycin to test whether the effect runs through mTOR

result.caption: Direction and rank order as reported across the two source studies, which also report increased growth in Drosophila tissue. The bars show p-S6K1 only, because rapamycin blocks 4E-BP1 phosphorylation just partly. Schematic, not measured values.

conclude: More Rheb is sufficient to raise mTORC1 output in these systems, and the effect runs through mTOR rather than around it.
Rheb sits downstream of the TSC complex and upstream of the kinase, which is what put it on the pathway diagram in the first place.
cannotConclude: What endogenous Rheb does. Sufficiency at a raised level and necessity at a normal level are different claims, and this design supports the first.
Which variable did the work: the amount of protein changed, and for a state-biased mutant the state changed as well.
Anything about location, which was not measured.
nodes.informative: Historically decisive for placing Rheb on the map, and weak for the question in front of you: two variables move together, and neither of them is position.

interpret.label: It supports my hypothesis
interpret.note: It supports the nucleotide arm being able to drive output. Notice what you have to add silently to get from there to ‘nucleotide state is what decides’: that the extra protein went where it was needed.

interpret.label: It weakens my hypothesis
interpret.note: For a strong localisation hypothesis, an output rise without any spatial manipulation is uncomfortable — unless the extra Rheb is also reaching the compartment, which nothing here measures.

interpret.label: It is inconclusive for my question
interpret.note: A fair reading, and the reason is worth naming: an overexpression experiment changes abundance, and abundance is a third candidate explanation you have not been tracking.

interpret.label: It introduces an alternative explanation
interpret.note: It does, and the next panel makes it concrete. Raising Rheb does not leave the rest of the network where it was.

nodes.opensNote: A result with a complication in it opens exactly two moves: measure the complication, or go and look somewhere else entirely.

event.title: New information
event.info: Raising Rheb does not only raise mTORC1 output. In the same work that placed Rheb downstream of TSC1/TSC2, Rheb overexpression also lowered PKB/AKT phosphorylation — the arm that was supposed to be the input.

options.label: Yes, substantially
options.note: This is the reading the design supports. The experiment did not change one arrow; it changed a network that contains a feedback loop, and the readout you measured sits downstream of both the change and the loop.

options.label: Possibly
options.note: Reasonable if you think the feedback is slow relative to the measurement. Say what would make you sure — a time course, or measuring p-AKT in the same lysate, turns ‘possibly’ into something checkable.

options.label: No
options.note: Hard to hold once the feedback is on the table: the input arm moved, so the cell you measured is not the control cell with one arrow strengthened. The feedback cannot explain the rise, because it points the other way, but it changes what the rise is a measurement of.

options.label: Not enough information
options.note: Also defensible, and it points at the missing measurement rather than at the missing knowledge: the experiment as run does not report the state of the insulin arm.

event.explain: mTORC1 output feeds back on upstream insulin signalling, so a cell with more Rheb is not the same cell with one arrow strengthened. The rise in p-S6K1 is a real observation either way. What needs care is the interpretation: attributing it specifically to more Rheb-GTP acting on mTORC1 requires the feedback arm to be held constant, or at least measured.
event.control: Measure p-AKT in the same lysate; use an acute, inducible increase rather than a stable line, so the network has less time to re-equilibrate; or use an endogenous knock-in so that abundance is not the variable at all.

falsify.prompt: Name the result that would weaken your model, then run it.

options.label: More Rheb leaves the output where it was
options.note: That would break the arrow from Rheb to the kinase, which is the one thing all four of your hypotheses currently assume. The most expensive result to receive, and the least likely.

options.label: Output rises, and rapamycin blocks the rise
options.note: What the two source studies report. It places the effect inside mTOR signalling; what it cannot place is whether abundance or nucleotide state did the work.

options.label: Output rises and rapamycin does not touch it
options.note: That would put the effect outside the kinase you are studying and turn this into a different investigation. Worth naming, because it is how a clean result rules a route out.

options.label: Nothing here would change my mind
options.note: Then notice what you are buying: an overexpression result moves two variables at once, so this step mostly generates the objection that the next one measures.

nodes.label: Measure p-AKT in the same lysates
nodes.equipment: The lysates you already have and one more antibody. The cheapest follow-up here, and the one that decides what the step above meant.
nodes.addresses: Whether the manipulation moved more than one arm of the network

design.model: The same cultured cells and the same lysates as the step above
design.perturbation: None new — this reads a second output from material you already have
design.control: Empty-vector lysates from the same experiment

result.caption: Direction as reported in the source study, which notes that Rheb overexpression lowers PKB/AKT phosphorylation. Schematic, not measured values.

conclude: The manipulation moved the input arm as well as the output, so what changed was a network with a feedback loop in it, not one arrow.
With the feedback measured rather than assumed, the size of the objection is on the record and the overexpression result can be stated with its scope attached.
cannotConclude: What the p-S6K1 rise would have been with the insulin arm held where it was. The feedback cannot have produced the rise, since lower p-AKT points the other way, but it means the rise was measured on a re-set network. Holding that arm constant needs an acute or endogenous manipulation, not another blot.
Anything about location — nothing here reports where any of these proteins were.
nodes.informative: Low on its own and high in combination. Fifteen units turn a result you could not interpret into one you can, which is the cheapest thing you will do in this challenge.

interpret.label: It supports my hypothesis
interpret.note: It supports being able to state your hypothesis carefully. A measured confounder is not a confirmed one — it is a known one.

interpret.label: It weakens my hypothesis
interpret.note: If you read the overexpression result as a clean single-variable experiment, yes. Notice the direction. Lower p-AKT would, on its own, lower mTORC1 output, so the feedback cannot be what produced the rise you measured. What it does show is that this is not a single-variable experiment: a cell with more Rheb is a cell with a re-set insulin arm, and the growth readout is downstream of both changes.

interpret.label: It is inconclusive for my question
interpret.note: It is clear about one thing: the design above is not a single-variable experiment. That is worth 15 units even though it answers nothing new about Rheb.

interpret.label: It introduces an alternative explanation
interpret.note: It confirms one that was already there. Feedback from mTORC1 onto the insulin arm is standard biology; this puts a number-free measurement next to it.

nodes.opensNote: With the feedback on the record you can go at the spatial arm without carrying an unresolved objection.

falsify.prompt: Before you read the second blot: what would change your mind about the step above?

options.label: p-AKT is unchanged — the manipulation moved one arrow after all
options.note: That would make the overexpression result a single-variable experiment and let you state it without a qualifier. It is the reading most people carry into this step.

options.label: p-AKT falls — the input arm moved too
options.note: What the source study reports. It does not explain the rise you measured, since lower input points the other way; it means the rise was measured on a network that had re-set itself.

options.label: p-AKT rises alongside Rheb
options.note: That would point at a loop running the other way and would need its own explanation. It is not what came out, and naming it is how you would have recognised it.

options.label: Nothing here would change my mind
options.note: Hard to hold for fifteen units. The whole value of this step is that it can change how the previous one reads — if it cannot, do not buy it.

nodes.label: Force mTORC1 to the lysosomal surface and remove the nutrient signal
nodes.equipment: Stable lines expressing Rag mutants, amino-acid withdrawal, western blot. Weeks of line-making before the first data point.
nodes.addresses: Position and nucleotide state against each other

design.perturbation: Express a GTP-locked Rag mutant that keeps mTORC1 at the lysosomal surface regardless of amino acids
design.readout: p-S6K1 with and without amino acids; mTOR localisation by imaging
design.control: Wild-type Rag at a matched expression level; a GDP-bound Rag mutant

result.caption: Direction and rank order as reported in the source study: locking the Rag mutant in its GTP-bound form made mTORC1 signalling resistant to amino-acid withdrawal. Schematic, not measured values.

conclude: Where mTORC1 sits is a control point in its own right: fix the position and the cell no longer needs the amino-acid signal to keep signalling.
The amino-acid arm and the growth-factor arm are doing different jobs — one moves the kinase, the other loads its activator.
cannotConclude: That position on its own is enough. These cells still had growth factors, and therefore an activator that was still loaded.
Anything about Rheb's nucleotide state in these cells, which was not measured in the same experiment.
That the mutant Rag behaves like an endogenous protein at an endogenous level — it is expressed, so its amount is a variable too.
nodes.informative: The most discriminating experiment on this menu, because the hypotheses predict different things here. A nucleotide-dominant view expects the amino-acid withdrawal to matter little either way; a localisation-dominant view expects exactly the pattern reported.

interpret.label: It supports my hypothesis
interpret.note: If you committed to localisation, this is the strongest support available in the corpus. Keep the qualifier in view: it shows the position requirement can be satisfied artificially, not that the loading requirement went away.

interpret.label: It weakens my hypothesis
interpret.note: For a strict nucleotide-dominant view it is awkward: withdrawing amino acids should not have mattered much, and in wild-type cells it did.

interpret.label: It is inconclusive for my question
interpret.note: Too cautious, but for a good reason: the experiment separates the amino-acid input from the output, and leaves the two requirements bundled together in the growth-factor-replete condition.

interpret.label: It introduces an alternative explanation
interpret.note: It reframes the question more than it answers it: position may be a gate that has to be open rather than a dial that sets the level.

nodes.opensNote: Once position is a control point, the questions become how far it goes and whether it is really separable.

falsify.prompt: This is the discriminating step. Which result would weaken the hypothesis you committed to?

options.label: Locking the position keeps signalling going without amino acids
options.note: What the source study reports, and the result a nucleotide-dominant reading has to absorb: position turns out to be doing work rather than keeping house.

options.label: Locking the position changes nothing — withdrawal still collapses the output
options.note: That would leave position as a housekeeping detail and hand the question to the nucleotide arm. It is the cleanest support a nucleotide-dominant reading could have got here.

options.label: Output collapses under every condition, locked or not
options.note: That would say the manipulation broke something other than what it aimed at, and the matched controls on this card are there to catch exactly that.

options.label: Nothing here would change my mind
options.note: Worth rereading the card before you commit to that: this is the one step whose result the four hypotheses predict differently, so it is the step most able to move you.

nodes.label: Watch where the brake goes when the inputs are withdrawn
nodes.equipment: Immunofluorescence microscopy and a panel of stress conditions — cheap reagents, expensive microscope time.
nodes.addresses: Whether the two arms are separate variables at all

design.perturbation: Withdraw amino acids, or growth factors, or apply other stresses
design.readout: TSC2 localisation by imaging, alongside mTORC1 output
design.control: Full medium; cells with the inputs restored

result.caption: Direction and rank order as reported in the source study, which finds that both inputs have to be present for TSC2 to stay cytoplasmic. Schematic, not measured values.

conclude: The brake is spatially regulated too: TSC2 moves to the compartment where Rheb and mTORC1 meet whenever an input is missing.
‘Nucleotide state’ and ‘location’ are not two independent variables, because the enzyme that sets the nucleotide state is itself positioned.
cannotConclude: That TSC2 is acting on Rheb at that location — imaging shows where a protein is, not what it is doing there.
Anything quantitative about Rheb loading, which this design does not measure.
nodes.informative: It reframes rather than answers. Run late, it turns a two-way question into a better-posed one; run first, it spends a quarter of the budget on a complication you cannot yet use.

interpret.label: It supports my hypothesis
interpret.note: It supports the ‘both, and not independent’ reading more than either single-arm hypothesis, because it shows the arms sharing a mechanism.

interpret.label: It weakens my hypothesis
interpret.note: It weakens both strong forms at once: neither arm is the clean, isolable variable that a dominance claim needs.

interpret.label: It is inconclusive for my question
interpret.note: In the narrow sense, yes — it measures neither loading nor mTORC1 position. In the wider sense it tells you the question may be badly posed, which is worth knowing.

interpret.label: It introduces an alternative explanation
interpret.note: It does, and it is the most interesting one available: what looks like two competing mechanisms may be one mechanism with a spatial and a biochemical face.

nodes.opensNote: There is one step left after this, and it is the one no study in this corpus has taken.

falsify.prompt: Say what would weaken your model here before the images come back.

options.label: TSC2 stays cytoplasmic whatever is withdrawn
options.note: That would keep state and place as two separate variables, which is what makes the original question well posed. It would be good news for whichever single-arm hypothesis you hold.

options.label: TSC2 accumulates at the lysosome whenever an input is missing
options.note: What the source study reports, and the result that complicates both single-arm readings at once: the enzyme that sets the nucleotide state is itself positioned.

options.label: TSC2 moves for amino acids but not for growth factors
options.note: That would split the two inputs and give you a sharper question than the one you started with. It is not what came out, and it would have been worth the twenty-five units.

options.label: Nothing here would change my mind
options.note: Then this step is a reframing you have decided not to accept in advance, which is a position rather than an argument — and an expensive one at this price.

nodes.label: Move Rheb itself, at endogenous levels, both ways
nodes.equipment: A knock-in line, reciprocal targeting constructs and live imaging. The most equipment on this menu, and part of why nobody in this corpus has done it.
nodes.addresses: Position alone at endogenous abundance. No study in this Atlas corpus reports it; published attempts relocalise re-expressed Rheb rather than the endogenous protein, and one of them finds Rheb is not enriched on lysosomes at all.

design.model: Cultured cells with a knock-in, so abundance is held at the endogenous level
design.perturbation: Tether Rheb to a defined membrane, and separately remove it from that membrane, leaving the nucleotide cycle intact
design.readout: p-S6K1 and p-4E-BP1, Rheb-GTP loading, and the localisation of both proteins in the same cells
design.control: Untethered knock-in carrying the same tag and linker

evidence.basis: No study in this Atlas corpus reports this experiment. What follows is the outcome the model above predicts, written as a prediction and labelled as one. Treat it as a hypothesis to be tested, not as a result to be cited.

bars.label: Rheb removed from the surface, still loaded

result.caption: Expected, not observed. These bars are what the teaching model predicts if position and loading are two requirements that both have to be met. Nothing in the Atlas corpus reports this measurement.

conclude: Only the reciprocal pair — adding the protein to a compartment and removing it from the same compartment — would let a spatial claim stand on its own.
Holding abundance at the endogenous level is what would separate this from the overexpression experiment above.
cannotConclude: Anything at all, until it is done. Reading a predicted pattern as evidence is the specific error this challenge is built to make visible.
A tether is itself a perturbation: the tag, the linker and the local concentration are three changes riding along with the one you meant to make.
nodes.informative: The highest in principle and the most expensive, and it is a gap in this corpus rather than a line in it. Choosing it costs 40 units and returns a prediction — which is a fair picture of what committing to an unpublished experiment actually feels like.

interpret.label: It supports my hypothesis
interpret.note: A prediction cannot support a hypothesis; it is generated by one. If this felt like support while you were reading it, that is the reflex the labelling is here to interrupt.

interpret.label: It weakens my hypothesis
interpret.note: Also not something a prediction can do. What it can do is tell you which hypothesis you would abandon if the experiment came out the other way.

interpret.label: It is inconclusive for my question
interpret.note: Correct, and the useful follow-up is: what would you have to see here to change your mind? Naming that in advance is most of what makes an experiment worth running.

interpret.label: It introduces an alternative explanation
interpret.note: It introduces a design problem rather than an explanation: the tether adds variables, so even the real version of this experiment would need its own controls.

rules.note: You closed the investigation without spending anything. That is a legitimate move only if you had already decided the menu could not move the question — and if so, the reasoning for that belongs in the last step.
The forced-location step is what did the work. It is the one place where a nucleotide-dominant reading and a location-dominant reading expect different things, and the result went against the first.

You never bought a step that varied position while the nucleotide arm stayed where it was. Without one, every result you have is compatible with either arm doing the work — which is why the question can still feel open at the end.

Running both spatial steps is the fullest picture available here: one shows position is a control point, the other shows the brake is positioned too. Together they say the original question was posed as a dichotomy that the mechanism does not respect.

Ten units went on the GAP assay. It is a clean experiment about a step none of your hypotheses disputed, so it bought confidence in shared background rather than a decision — the cheapest way to feel like you are making progress. It is also what opens the two cell-based steps, so it is not wasted; it is just not an answer to the question you asked.

You ran the overexpression step and left its complication unmeasured. Fifteen units — the cheapest follow-up on the menu — would have turned a result you cannot interpret into one you can, and it is the reason that sub-question stayed unanswered.

You measured the confounder instead of assuming it away. Fifteen units did more for the interpretability of your route than any other step on the menu, which is roughly how control experiments work in practice.

Forty units — the largest single item — bought a prediction rather than a result, and the card said so before you paid. That makes it a decision rather than a trap, and it is what committing to an unpublished experiment actually costs.
Everything you ran sits on the nucleotide arm. Those steps are consistent with each other, and consistency between experiments that test the same thing is not evidence against the alternative.

model.title: The model you are arguing with
model.caption: Two lanes converge on the same kinase. The upper lane is the growth-factor arm that sets Rheb's nucleotide state; the lower lane is the nutrient arm that decides whether mTORC1 is recruited to the lysosomal surface at all. The location control stands for that lower lane being engaged or not. Nodes and arrows are taken from the Atlas pathway model, so this teaching diagram cannot drift away from the scientific one.

controls.label: Growth factors
options: ON
OFF

controls.label: Rheb nucleotide state
options: GTP
GDP

controls.label: mTORC1 location
options: lysosome
cytosol

ON|GTP|lysosome.note: Both conditions are met at once: the activator is loaded and the kinase is where the activator is. This is the state every hypothesis on your list predicts, which is exactly why it cannot tell them apart.

ON|GTP|cytosol.note: Sit with this one. The hormone is present, the brake is released, Rheb is loaded — and the output is still low, because the kinase is not at the place where the activating step happens. If you hold that nucleotide state alone determines the output, this state is the one you have to explain away.

ON|GDP|lysosome.note: The mirror image, and the reason recruitment is not the same thing as activation: mTORC1 arrives at the surface, finds an unloaded activator, and does nothing. Docking is a precondition, not the switch.

ON|GDP|cytosol.note: Neither condition is met. Note that the readout is identical to the two states above it — one blot cannot tell you which of the two requirements was the one that failed.

OFF|GTP|lysosome.note: Rheb stays loaded with no hormone present. The model holds this state so you can compare it with the one below; in a cell it corresponds to a TSC-null background, where the brake is absent rather than merely unengaged.

OFF|GTP|cytosol.note: The same loaded Rheb as the state above, and no output, because the kinase is elsewhere. Read the two together: they are the cleanest statement this model can make that position is doing work of its own.

OFF|GDP|lysosome.note: Nutrients are there, the hormone is not, the brake is engaged and Rheb has unloaded. mTORC1 sits on the surface waiting for an input that is not coming.

OFF|GDP|cytosol.note: The resting or starved state: no permission signal, brake engaged, activator unloaded, kinase not recruited, autophagy no longer restrained.

break.prompt: Break the brake. Take away the growth-factor signal and, at the same time, disable the TSC complex so Rheb stays GTP-loaded. What does the model do?
options: Output stays low — without a hormone the kinase cannot fire
Output is high, as long as mTORC1 is still recruited to the lysosome
Output is high whatever the location, because loaded Rheb is the switch
The model cannot represent this
break.explain: Removing the brake keeps Rheb loaded, so the growth-factor input becomes dispensable — but only in the states where mTORC1 is at the surface. Switch the location control to cytosol and the same loaded Rheb produces nothing. This is a prediction about the teaching model, not a measurement; the experiments below are where measurements come in.

break.prompt: Now remove the spatial component instead: leave growth factors on and Rheb GTP-loaded, and stop mTORC1 being recruited. What does that state tell you about the claim ‘Rheb-GTP determines mTORC1 activity’?
options: It supports the claim, because Rheb is still loaded
It weakens the claim as stated, because loading is present and output is not
It is irrelevant to the claim
It shows Rheb is not involved at all
break.explain: The claim as written says loading determines output. The model produces a state with loading and without output, so the claim needs a qualifier: Rheb-GTP determines the output given that mTORC1 is where Rheb is. Adding that qualifier is not a retreat — it is the more testable version of the same idea.

break.prompt: Three different states in this model give an identical p-S6K1 readout. What follows for an experiment that measures only p-S6K1?
options: Nothing — p-S6K1 is the standard readout of mTORC1 activity
A low p-S6K1 alone does not tell you which requirement failed, so the design needs a second measurement that differs between the candidates
p-S6K1 should be replaced by p-4E-BP1 in every design
The model is wrong, because one readout should distinguish one cause
break.explain: This is the whole idea of experiment informativeness in one picture. A readout is useful in proportion to how differently the competing explanations predict it. p-S6K1 is a fine readout of output; it is a poor discriminator here, because three quite different states of the cell produce the same value. What separates them is measuring the nucleotide state or the localisation as well.

hypotheses.prompt: Commit to a working hypothesis before you spend anything. It is meant to be revised later — that is what the last step of this challenge is for.

options.label: Nucleotide state is dominant
options.note: The strong version of the textbook arrow: what the kinase reads is whether Rheb carries GTP, and everything upstream matters only through that. It predicts that any manipulation raising Rheb-GTP raises output, and that position is a housekeeping detail. The state to watch is growth factors ON, Rheb-GTP, mTORC1 cytosolic — if that gives no output, this hypothesis needs a qualifier.

options.label: Localisation is dominant
options.note: The spatial version: the regulated step is whether mTORC1 is brought to the surface where its activator waits, and the nucleotide cycle is largely permissive. It predicts that forcing the location makes the nutrient input dispensable — which is close to what one of the experiments below reports. Its weak point is that forcing the location in a growth-factor-replete cell leaves loading untested.

options.label: Both contribute, and they are not independent
options.note: Two requirements that have to be met together, with the added twist that the brake itself relocates. It is the most defensible reading of the current evidence and the hardest to test, because ‘both matter’ only becomes a scientific claim once you say what would change if one of them did not.

options.label: The current evidence does not separate them
options.note: A legitimate position rather than a refusal to answer. It commits you to naming the missing experiment, which is what the last step of this challenge asks for. Hold it seriously and you should be reluctant to spend your budget on experiments that every hypothesis predicts identically.

revise.prompt: Your working hypothesis, after the evidence you bought
revise.note: Changing your mind here is the expected outcome, not a failure state. A first hypothesis that survives every experiment untouched usually means the experiments were not discriminating.

feedback.nucleotide: Holding the nucleotide arm as dominant after these results means committing to a qualifier: loading decides the output given that the kinase is at the surface. That is a narrower and better claim than the one you started with.
feedback.localisation: The forced-location experiment is the strongest support in the corpus for this reading. What it does not give you is the reciprocal: those cells still had growth factors, so the loading requirement was quietly satisfied throughout.
feedback.both: The most defensible reading of what you have seen, and the one that inherits the hardest job: making ‘both’ specific enough to test. The brake-localisation result is the reason it is not simply a hedge.
feedback.insufficient: A position with a duty attached: name the experiment that would separate them. The one this challenge could not buy you a result for is the reciprocal targeting of Rheb at endogenous levels.

compare.whatTheyTested: Whether the Rag GTPases are the missing link between amino acids and mTORC1 — measured as binding to raptor, as mTOR's position inside the cell, and as whether a GTP-locked Rag makes signalling resistant to amino-acid withdrawal.
whatItAnswered: Amino acids act on mTORC1 largely by moving it to a compartment that also holds its activator.
Fixing that position artificially removes the cell's need for the amino-acid signal.
The Rag proteins do not themselves switch on the kinase activity — the recruitment step and the activation step are separable.
whatItDidNot: It did not measure Rheb's nucleotide state in those cells, so the two arms were not separated within one experiment.
The Rag mutants are expressed rather than endogenous, so their abundance is a variable alongside their state.
It shows that reaching the compartment is required, not that being in the compartment is by itself enough.
compare.howToRead: The published experiment is not the perfect version of your design, and it was never meant to be. It is a real design with its own controls, its own scope and its own limits — and reading it that way, rather than as a verdict, is the skill this step is for. Compare it with what you chose: which of your unspent experiments would you now run alongside it?

reflection.prompt: What changed your mind, if anything?
options: A result came out differently from what I predicted
A result was what I expected but did not distinguish the hypotheses
A limitation or confounder made me re-read a result I had already accepted
Nothing changed; I ended where I started

reflection.prompt: Which evidence mattered most to your final position?
options: The forced-location experiment
The overexpression result, once the feedback was on the table
The spatial regulation of the brake
The absence of the experiment I most wanted to run

nextQuestion.text: The list above is where a next experiment would go. Pick the one you would actually defend in front of someone holding the budget — not the most interesting one, the one that would change what the field can claim.
nextQuestion.prompt: You have one more opportunity and a limited budget. What would you do next?

options.label: Build the reciprocal targeting experiment for Rheb at endogenous levels
options.note: The direct attack on the gap. Expensive, slow, and the only option that turns the spatial claim into something with its own controls. Budget the reciprocal arm from the start — a one-directional tether leaves the result ambiguous.

options.label: Measure loading and localisation in the same cells, under one set of conditions
options.note: Cheaper and often underrated. Much of the difficulty here comes from arms measured in different cells on different days; a single matched dataset would not settle the question but would tell you how far apart the arms really are.

options.label: Repeat the forced-location experiment with growth factors withdrawn
options.note: The missing cell of the existing design. If fixed position still gives output without a growth-factor signal, position is doing more work than the current reading allows; if it does not, the two-requirement model gains real support.

options.label: Test whether the brake's relocation is required for the output change
options.note: Follows the most interesting complication rather than the original question. Blocking TSC2's move while leaving its activity intact is hard to do cleanly, which is worth knowing before you commit the budget.

relatedRoutes.why: The growth-factor route, which is the nucleotide arm drawn end to end.
The amino-acid route, which is the spatial arm drawn end to end.

answer.short: On the evidence in this Atlas: no, not on its own. Rheb behaves as one of two requirements that have to be met at the same time — the kinase has to be at the compartment, and the activator it meets there has to be loaded.

observation.text: TSC2 accelerates the conversion of Rheb-GTP to Rheb-GDP, and cells without a working TSC complex hold more Rheb-GTP and more mTOR signalling.
Insulin raises Rheb-GTP loading in cells in a PI3K-dependent way, and TSC1/TSC2 blocks that rise.
Raising Rheb raises S6K1 and 4E-BP1 phosphorylation and drives growth in the systems where it was tested.
A GTP-locked Rag mutant holds mTORC1 at the lysosomal surface and makes its signalling resistant to amino-acid withdrawal.
TSC2 itself accumulates on lysosomes whenever amino acids or growth factors are missing.

interpretation: Read together, these support a two-requirement model rather than a single switch. Nutrients decide where the kinase is; growth factors decide whether the activator waiting there is loaded. Neither arm produces output without the other, which is why the model in step 2 has two states with an identical readout and completely different causes.

Rheb is still the step the kinase reads directly, which is why the ON/OFF language stuck to it. What the evidence does not support is the stronger version: that the nucleotide state by itself sets the output regardless of where the kinase is.

The two arms are not independent either, because the enzyme that sets the nucleotide state is itself positioned — TSC2 moves to the same compartment when an input is withdrawn. So ‘state versus place’ is a useful way to design an experiment and a poor way to describe the mechanism.
stillOpen: No study in this corpus moves Rheb itself between compartments at endogenous levels while leaving its nucleotide cycle intact. That is the reciprocal experiment the question actually asks for, and it is the 40-unit item on your menu that returns a prediction instead of a result.

The relative contribution of the two arms in one cell at one moment is measured nowhere: the arms were established in separate experiments, often in different cell types, and comparing across them is comparing designs as much as biology.
Several of the foundational nucleotide-state results used overexpressed protein, so how much of the effect survives at endogenous abundance is an open question rather than a settled detail.

hypothesisVerdicts.nucleotide: Survives only with a qualifier: Rheb-GTP determines the output given that mTORC1 is at the compartment. The forced-location experiment is what forces the qualifier, and the qualified version is the more testable claim — so this is a hypothesis that got sharper rather than one that failed.
hypothesisVerdicts.localisation: Half-right in a way worth naming. Position is a genuine control point, but the experiment that shows it was run in growth-factor-replete cells, so the loading requirement was quietly satisfied the whole time. Nothing here shows position is sufficient on its own.
hypothesisVerdicts.both: The reading the current evidence best supports, and the one that inherits the hardest job: making ‘both’ specific enough to test. The brake-localisation result is what saves it from being a hedge — it names a shared mechanism rather than just declining to choose.
hypothesisVerdicts.insufficient: Defensible for the narrow question of relative contribution, which really is unmeasured. Harder to hold for the broad question, because the forced-location result does decide something: it rules out the version where position is a housekeeping detail.

challenges.title: Why rapamycin does not switch mTORC1 off
challenges.subtitle: One drug, two complexes, and a clock — and how you would tell which of the three you are looking at
challenges.researchQuestion: Cells treated with rapamycin keep doing some of the things mTORC1 drives. Is that because of how the drug inhibits, because of what the experiment measures, because the network answers back, or because the drug is acting somewhere else?

prerequisites.why: What the kinase integrates, and which readouts stand in for its activity.
Why a sentence about ‘mTOR inhibition’ is usually a sentence about one of two complexes.
The loops that make a treated cell something other than an untreated cell with one arrow cut.
Reading a single band as a claim about a whole pathway is the habit this challenge works against.

learningObjectives: Distinguish a claim about a drug's target from a claim about which of that target's outputs it blocks
Predict which readout would hide a partial block and which would expose it
Rank candidate experiments by how well they separate a property of the drug from a response of the network
Identify what a single-arm dose-escalation trial can and cannot support

whatWeKnow.claim: Rapamycin does not work alone. It binds the small abundant protein FKBP12, and the pair docks on a site next to the kinase's active site rather than in it, so the inhibition is steric obstruction rather than occupancy of the catalytic pocket.
The S6K1 arm goes quiet within minutes of treatment, and that band is the readout most papers use when they report ‘mTORC1 activity’.
Compared against an inhibitor that occupies the active site, rapamycin leaves a class of mTORC1 outputs largely running — 4E-BP1 phosphorylation most of all, and autophagy induction as well.

Time changes the target list. Short exposure leaves the second complex alone; prolonged exposure traps free mTOR and new mTORC2 stops being assembled in the sensitive lines, and the same loss of signalling appears in mouse liver.
Inhibiting mTORC1 releases a brake on the arm above it: S6K1 no longer represses IRS-1, upstream receptor signalling picks up, and Akt activity can rise rather than fall.
A bivalent molecule can reach the substrate rapamycin leaves alone while leaving the second complex largely engaged, in resistant breast-cancer models and in a first-in-human dose-escalation trial.

uncertainty: Whether prolonged exposure reaches the second complex in any particular cell depends on the line, the dose and the duration. The Atlas grades that edge as contested for a reason: it is absent acutely and variably present later.

Two routes lead from mTORC1 inhibition to disturbed glucose handling — loss of the second complex and relief of the S6K1-to-IRS-1 brake — and their relative contribution has never been apportioned in people.

The lifespan data in this corpus come from rapamycin, and the selective compounds have been read out against tumour endpoints. No study here joins selective inhibition to an ageing outcome, which is the join the last sub-question asks for.

budget.note: Each step costs what its equipment costs. Running everything would take 205 units, and answering every sub-question that can be answered would take 165 — so this budget buys four of the five answers at most. Which four is the whole exercise.

lab.startNote: Three ways in: the cheap historical blot, the chemistry comparison that does the discriminating, or straight at the network's reply. None of them is wrong, and they do not cost the same.

goals.question: Does rapamycin block every mTORC1 output to the same degree?
goals.note: Three findings, and that is the point: one band tells you the drug engages its target, two bands tell you the block is uneven, and a functional readout tells you the unevenness is not an antibody story.

goals.question: Is a deeper block chemically available, or is this as far as the kinase can be pushed?
Does the network answer back when mTORC1 is inhibited?
Does the drug reach the second complex, and does that depend on time?
Can the metabolic cost be separated from target engagement?
goals.note: Two ways of separating them — by calendar and by molecule — and neither is worth much without the other, because one shows the cost shrinking and the other shows it being designed out.

goals.question: Does a block that spares the second complex keep the lifespan benefit without the metabolic cost?
goals.note: Nothing in this corpus yields this. The only step that would address it returns a prediction rather than a result, so this sub-question stays open at any price — and it is the same gap the Atlas records as H2, not an omission from the menu.

nodes.label: Treat cells with rapamycin and blot p-S6K1
nodes.equipment: Cell culture, one compound, one antibody. The oldest experiment in this field and still the cheapest item on the menu.
nodes.addresses: Whether the drug reaches mTORC1 at all

design.model: Cultured mammalian cells and T cells
design.perturbation: Add rapamycin to growing cells for tens of minutes
design.control: Untreated cells, and vehicle without the compound

result.caption: Direction and rank order as reported in the two source studies. The bars are a schematic of that direction, not measured values.

conclude: Rapamycin reaches mTORC1 and takes the S6K1 arm down within minutes.
The drug has a real molecular target in this pathway, which is why it became the tool the whole field was built on.
cannotConclude: Anything about the outputs you did not blot for. One band is one substrate.
Whether mTORC1 as a whole went quiet, which is the question you actually asked.
nodes.informative: High for the existence of the target and zero for your question: all four hypotheses predict this band collapsing. Ten units buy confidence in shared background rather than a decision — though these are also the lysates the next step reads, so it is not money thrown away.

interpret.label: It supports my hypothesis
interpret.note: Be careful what it supports. A result every candidate explanation predicts favours none of them; it agrees with the part nobody was disputing, which feels like progress and is not.

interpret.label: It weakens my hypothesis
interpret.note: Hard to see how. No hypothesis on your list denies that rapamycin takes the S6K1 arm down — they differ about what the rest of the kinase is doing while that happens.

interpret.label: It is inconclusive for my question
interpret.note: That is the reading this result deserves. A clean, interpretable experiment about a step none of your four explanations disagreed on.

interpret.label: It introduces an alternative explanation
interpret.note: Not an alternative so much as a reminder of how the habit started: this band is fast, cheap and dramatic, which is exactly why it became the readout everyone reported.

nodes.opensNote: One lysate, two antibodies: the second substrate is the cheapest next move. The drug comparison becomes worth its price once you know the drug engages its target.

falsify.prompt: Before the blot comes back: which result would weaken the model you are holding?

options.label: p-S6K1 is unchanged — the drug never reaches the kinase
options.note: That would end the investigation and start a different one. It is the result none of your four hypotheses can absorb, which makes it the honest answer to what would change your mind — and the least likely one to arrive.

options.label: p-S6K1 collapses within minutes
options.note: What the two source studies report, and what all four of your hypotheses predict. A result everyone expects cannot weaken anybody, so naming it here is a sign the step is background rather than evidence.

options.label: p-S6K1 falls only after days of treatment
options.note: That would make this a slow, indirect effect and would put the time axis in play far earlier than it belongs. Worth naming, because it is how you would have spotted it.

options.label: Nothing here would change my mind
options.note: The most defensible answer on this card, and it comes with a cost attached: if no outcome would move you, the ten units are buying a lysate rather than an argument.

nodes.label: Probe the same lysates for p-4E-BP1
nodes.equipment: The lysates you already have and one more antibody. No new cells, no new dosing.
nodes.addresses: Whether the block is the same size on every output

design.model: The same cultured cells and the same lysates as the step above
design.perturbation: None new — this reads a second substrate from material you already have
design.control: Untreated lysates from the same experiment, run on the same blot

result.unit: Phosphorylation of two substrates under rapamycin
result.caption: Direction and rank order as reported in the source studies, which describe 4E-BP1 phosphorylation as largely surviving a treatment that collapses S6K1. Schematic, not measured values.

conclude: The drug is substrate-selective rather than a general off-switch: one arm goes, the other largely stays.
A single-substrate readout reports the size of the block on that substrate, and nothing wider.
cannotConclude: Why the two arms differ. A blot shows the difference; the mechanism behind it needs a second chemistry or a structure.
Whether the residue is a property of the drug or a response of the network, since both were free to happen in this dish.
nodes.informative: The best value on the menu. Fifteen units turn ‘the drug engages its target’ into ‘the drug engages it unevenly’, which is the observation the rest of this challenge is about. It also puts the readout-artefact hypothesis under real pressure for the first time.

interpret.label: It supports my hypothesis
interpret.note: If you chose partial block, this is the observation your hypothesis exists to explain. Notice it is an observation and not yet a mechanism: nothing here says why the two substrates differ.

interpret.label: It weakens my hypothesis
interpret.note: For the readout-artefact reading it is awkward: the residue is on a second antibody, in the same lysate, under the same dose, so it is not a property of one reagent.

interpret.label: It is inconclusive for my question
interpret.note: Too cautious now. The split between arms is the thing that needs explaining, and you have it for 25 units in total.

interpret.label: It introduces an alternative explanation
interpret.note: It does, quietly: if one arm survives, perhaps the kinase was never fully blocked, and perhaps the cell helped. Those are two different follow-ups, and they cost different amounts.

nodes.opensNote: Two ways on from an uneven block: bring in a chemistry that blocks differently, or check whether the unevenness reaches the arm the drug is famous for.

falsify.prompt: Name the outcome that would weaken your hypothesis, then read the second antibody.

options.label: Both substrates collapse together
options.note: That would make the drug a clean off-switch and leave the residue everyone argues about as an artefact of somebody's blot. It is the strongest result the readout-artefact reading could have received.

options.label: S6K1 collapses while 4E-BP1 largely survives
options.note: What the source studies report. It is the observation the rest of this challenge exists to explain, and the first real pressure on a readout-artefact reading.

options.label: 4E-BP1 collapses while S6K1 survives
options.note: The mirror image, and it would overturn a decade of reading. Naming it is useful precisely because it shows which way round the asymmetry runs.

options.label: Nothing here would change my mind
options.note: Then you are treating the split as decided before you have seen it, which is the habit this step is cheapest at interrupting.

nodes.label: Compare rapamycin head to head with an active-site inhibitor
nodes.equipment: A second compound, matched dose-response for both, and a full substrate panel. New chemistry, so a new cost.
nodes.addresses: Whether the incompleteness belongs to the drug or to the kinase

design.model: Mouse and human cell lines, including primary cells
design.perturbation: Treat matched cultures with rapamycin or with an ATP-competitive inhibitor
design.control: Vehicle-treated cultures, and a dose-response for each compound so the comparison is not a dose artefact

result.caption: Direction and rank order as reported in the two source studies, which used the active-site compound as a ruler against rapamycin. Schematic, not measured values.

conclude: A deeper block is chemically available, so what rapamycin leaves running is a property of how rapamycin inhibits rather than a limit of the kinase.
The rapamycin-resistant outputs are only visible when a second chemistry is there to measure against — which is why the field lived with them for a decade.
cannotConclude: That the deeper block is the better drug. This design reads substrate phosphorylation, not benefit and not harm.
Which complex each compound is acting on: the same active site sits in both, so this chemistry has no reason to tell them apart.
nodes.informative: The most discriminating step at a middling price. The two chemistries are predicted to behave differently by the partial-block reading and identically by the readout-artefact one, so the result separates them — and it says nothing about the time axis or about the network's reply.

interpret.label: It supports my hypothesis
interpret.note: For partial block, strongly, and with a scope worth stating: two chemistries, one panel of substrates, in cells. What it does not give you is the size of that difference in a tissue.

interpret.label: It weakens my hypothesis
interpret.note: For readout-artefact it is close to decisive: the residue moves when the molecule changes while the antibodies stay the same, which is not how a reagent artefact behaves.

interpret.label: It is inconclusive for my question
interpret.note: Defensible only in a narrow sense — relief of feedback happens under both compounds, so this design does not take that contribution off the table.

interpret.label: It introduces an alternative explanation
interpret.note: It introduces a cost rather than an explanation: a compound that reaches further reaches into the second complex as well, and that is the trade-off the last two steps are about.

nodes.opensNote: Having a ruler makes two further questions affordable: how far the unevenness extends across outputs, and what happens when the drug stays on.

falsify.prompt: This is the discriminating step. Which result would weaken the hypothesis you committed to?

options.label: Both compounds stop at the same depth
options.note: That would make the residue a property of the kinase rather than of the drug, and a partial-block reading would lose its main claim. It is the result that reading has to be willing to receive.

options.label: The active-site compound reaches further than rapamycin
options.note: What both source studies report. The residue moves when the molecule changes while the antibodies stay the same, which is the pattern a readout artefact cannot produce.

options.label: Rapamycin reaches further than the active-site compound
options.note: That would be a surprise worth chasing and would say something is wrong with the dosing or the compound rather than with the model. The dose-response on this card exists to tell those apart.

options.label: Nothing here would change my mind
options.note: Twenty-five units is a lot to spend on a result you have decided in advance. If that is where you are, the cheaper steps are the better buy.

nodes.label: Ask whether the autophagy arm is released the way textbooks say
nodes.equipment: Flux assays with lysosomal blockade, imaging and blots. Cheap reagents, fussy controls, and a fortnight of them.
nodes.addresses: Whether the uneven block reaches the arm the drug is best known for

design.perturbation: Rapamycin or an active-site inhibitor, each with and without lysosomal blockade
design.readout: Autophagic flux rather than a single marker at a single time point
design.control: Untreated cells, plus the blockade-only arm that makes flux readable at all

result.caption: Direction and rank order as reported in the source study, which found autophagy among the mTORC1 outputs rapamycin leaves largely intact. Schematic, not measured values.

conclude: ‘Rapamycin induces autophagy’ needs a qualifier: the induction is partial, and the compound that occupies the active site induces more.
The unevenness is not confined to translation. It shows up on the arm most often quoted as the drug's main effect, which is where it does the most damage to sloppy reading.
cannotConclude: How much of this carries into a tissue, where the dose at the cell and the supply of nutrients are both different.
That the difference between compounds on this arm runs through mTORC1 alone, since the active-site compound is not complex-selective.
nodes.informative: Moderate for the question as posed and high for unlearning a sentence most readers arrive with. It is also the step whose price is easiest to underestimate: flux needs the blockade arm, and without it you are measuring a marker, not recycling.

interpret.label: It supports my hypothesis
interpret.note: For partial block, yes, and it widens the claim from one substrate to a functional output — which is a stronger position than a second band on the same blot.

interpret.label: It weakens my hypothesis
interpret.note: For readout-artefact it is the harder result of the two, because this is not a phosphosite. A functional readout behaving like the phosphosites leaves little room for an antibody story.

interpret.label: It is inconclusive for my question
interpret.note: A fair reading if your question was about the residue on 4E-BP1 specifically. This step widens the phenomenon rather than explaining it.

interpret.label: It introduces an alternative explanation
interpret.note: It reframes more than it explains: the drug does not turn mTORC1 output down by a fixed fraction, it reshapes which outputs stay on. That is a different kind of pharmacology from a dial.

nodes.opensNote: Once the unevenness is established across arms, the open question is what the same molecule does when it stays on for days.

falsify.prompt: Before the flux assay: what would weaken your model?

options.label: Both compounds induce recycling to the same extent
options.note: That would confine the unevenness to translation and leave the drug's best-known effect intact. It is the result that would keep the textbook sentence as it stands.

options.label: Rapamycin induces it partly, and the active-site compound more
options.note: What the source study reports. A functional readout behaving like the phosphosites leaves a readout-artefact reading with very little room.

options.label: Neither compound induces recycling at all
options.note: That would say the block on this arm is not being relieved by either chemistry, and it would point the investigation at the assay before it pointed at the biology.

options.label: Nothing here would change my mind
options.note: Then twenty units buy a wider description of something you already accept. That is a legitimate purchase and a poor one at this stage.

nodes.label: Follow the arm above the kinase after mTORC1 is inhibited
nodes.equipment: Cell culture, a time course, and antibodies against p-AKT and IRS-1. Cheap, and the design is in the time points rather than the reagents.
nodes.addresses: Whether the network replies when the kinase is blocked

design.perturbation: Inhibit mTORC1 and follow the upstream arm over a time course rather than at one point
design.readout: p-AKT and IRS-1 levels alongside p-S6K1
design.control: Untreated cultures sampled at the same time points

result.caption: Direction as reported across the source studies, which describe relief of feedback onto receptor signalling and a biphasic rise in Akt phosphorylation. Schematic, not measured values.

conclude: Inhibiting the kinase releases a brake on the arm above it, so the cell you measure an hour later is not the untreated cell with one arrow cut.
Part of what reads as an incomplete block is the network pushing back, which is a different thing from a drug obstructing a substrate channel.
cannotConclude: How much of the surviving 4E-BP1 phosphorylation is feedback and how much is substrate selectivity. Separating those needs the chemistry comparison, not this blot.
Anything about the second complex, which this design does not read, even though the arm to Akt runs through it.
nodes.informative: Cheap and clarifying. It puts a second contributor on the table with a measurement attached rather than leaving it as an objection raised after the talk — and it is the only step that discriminates the feedback hypothesis at all.

interpret.label: It supports my hypothesis
interpret.note: For the feedback reading, directly. Keep the limit in view: showing that a loop re-sets is not the same as showing how much of the residue it accounts for.

interpret.label: It weakens my hypothesis
interpret.note: For partial block in its strictest form it is uncomfortable, because now two things change when you add the drug. Most of the strength survives if you treat feedback as a co-contributor rather than a rival.

interpret.label: It is inconclusive for my question
interpret.note: Reasonable: the design shows a loop moving without apportioning the residue between two mechanisms. Saying what would apportion it is the useful next sentence.

interpret.label: It introduces an alternative explanation
interpret.note: It makes an existing one measurable, and it carries a warning for later: relief of this brake is one of two routes from mTORC1 inhibition to disturbed glucose handling, and the two have never been separated in people.

nodes.opensNote: With the network's reply on the record, the expensive question is what happens when the drug stays on long enough for the cell to rebuild itself around it.

falsify.prompt: Say what would weaken your model before you follow the arm above the kinase.

options.label: Upstream signalling sits still while mTORC1 goes down
options.note: That would take the network's reply off the table and leave the residue entirely to the chemistry. It is the cleanest result a partial-block reading could have received here.

options.label: p-AKT rises while p-S6K1 falls
options.note: What the source studies report. It does not explain the residue by itself, and it does mean the cell you measured is not the untreated cell with one arrow cut.

options.label: p-AKT falls together with p-S6K1
options.note: That would make the drug look like a general dampener of the whole arm and would need a different mechanism from the loops in the lessons. It is not what came out.

options.label: Nothing here would change my mind
options.note: This is the only step on the menu that can move the feedback hypothesis at all. Declining to be moved by it makes the other fifteen units the better buy.

nodes.label: Hold the drug on for days and read the second complex
nodes.equipment: Long-term culture across several lines, complex immunoprecipitation and the Ser473 antibody. Weeks of dosing before the first informative point.
nodes.addresses: Whether exposure time changes which complex the drug is acting on

design.model: Several human and mouse cell lines
design.perturbation: Short exposure against prolonged exposure to the same compound at the same dose
design.readout: Assembly of the second complex, and Akt Ser473 phosphorylation
design.control: Acutely treated and untreated cultures of the same lines, read on the same day

result.caption: Direction and rank order as reported in the source studies, in which prolonged treatment reduced assembly of the second complex in sensitive lines. Schematic, not measured values.

conclude: The drug's target list depends on how long it has been on: acutely the second complex is left alone, and after prolonged exposure new complex stops being assembled.
Any description of what this molecule blocks is unfinished without a duration attached, which is most of why two honest groups can report different target lists.
cannotConclude: That this happens in every cell type or at every dose. The reported sensitivity varies between lines, and the effect is dose- and duration-dependent, which is why the Atlas grades this edge contested.
That losing the second complex is what produces any whole-body effect — that needs an animal rather than a lysate.
nodes.informative: High, and it is the reason this challenge has a second axis at all. It separates the wrong-complex reading from the other three, and it leaves the residue on 4E-BP1 exactly where it was, since that sits inside mTORC1 signalling.

interpret.label: It supports my hypothesis
interpret.note: For the wrong-complex reading, yes — with the scope the Atlas itself attaches: sensitive lines, prolonged exposure, and an edge graded contested rather than settled background.

interpret.label: It weakens my hypothesis
interpret.note: For any reading that treats the drug as having one fixed target, this is the awkward result. The molecule did not change between the two lanes; only the clock did.

interpret.label: It is inconclusive for my question
interpret.note: Defensible if your question was strictly about the residue on mTORC1 outputs. This step answers a neighbouring question that turns out to matter more for what the drug does to an animal.

interpret.label: It introduces an alternative explanation
interpret.note: It introduces a second axis rather than an alternative: chemistry decides depth, and duration decides breadth. Most confusion in this literature comes from reporting one and reading the other.

nodes.opensNote: A time-dependent effect invites two quite different moves: change the schedule, or change the molecule. They cost different amounts and answer different questions.

event.title: New information
event.info: The same loss of second-complex signalling turns up in mouse liver, where prolonged treatment goes together with disturbed glucose handling — and in the same work, reducing mTORC1 signalling genetically, without the drug, extended lifespan in female mice without that metabolic cost.

options.label: Yes, substantially
options.note: This is the reading the design supports. The benefit and the metabolic cost come apart in that experiment, so ‘what does the drug block’ stops being one question and becomes two, with different answers and different consequences.

options.label: Possibly
options.note: Reasonable if you doubt how far a liver lysate travels. Say what would move you — matching target engagement between the genetic and the drug arms is the comparison that would make the separation readable.

options.label: No
options.note: Hard to hold once the genetic arm is on the table: it reaches the lifespan endpoint without the glucose phenotype, so attributing both to one undifferentiated ‘mTOR inhibition’ no longer fits what was measured.

options.label: Not enough information
options.note: Also defensible, and it points at a missing measurement rather than missing knowledge: what is absent is a matched comparison of schedules and molecules against the same endpoints in the same animals.

event.explain: Two things that had travelled together in the literature separate here. Reduced mTORC1 signalling reached the survival endpoint, while the metabolic cost tracked the loss of the second complex — which reframes the question from ‘how much does the drug inhibit’ to ‘which parts, for how long, and at what cost’. The separation is reported in mice, so it is a strong lead about mechanism rather than a statement about people.
event.control: Vary the schedule at a matched dose and read target engagement and glucose handling in the same animals; or hold the schedule and change the molecule to one that spares the second complex. Both of those are on the menu below.

falsify.prompt: Before the long exposure comes back: which result would weaken your model?

options.label: Prolonged exposure looks exactly like acute exposure
options.note: That would remove the time axis from the story and make the drug's target list a fixed property. A wrong-complex reading would lose most of its force, and the challenge would have one axis instead of two.

options.label: Prolonged exposure lowers Akt Ser473 while acute exposure leaves it alone
options.note: What the source studies report, with the scope the Atlas attaches: sensitive lines, prolonged exposure, an edge graded contested rather than background.

options.label: Even acute exposure lowers Akt Ser473
options.note: That would make the second complex an immediate target and would sit badly against the acute experiments in the rest of the corpus. Naming it is how you would have noticed a dose or a line behaving unusually.

options.label: Nothing here would change my mind
options.note: Thirty units on a foregone conclusion is the most expensive way to be certain on this menu. If the time axis cannot move you, spend it on the chemistry instead.

nodes.label: Change the schedule rather than the molecule
nodes.equipment: Mouse cohorts on different dosing intervals, glucose and pyruvate tolerance tests. Cheap only because the cohorts already exist.
nodes.addresses: Whether the metabolic cost can be separated from target engagement by timing alone

design.model: Mice dosed daily, weekly, or every fifth day
design.perturbation: Vary the dosing interval at a matched dose
design.readout: Glucose and pyruvate tolerance, fasting insulin, beta-cell function, alongside mTORC1 output
design.control: Untreated littermates, and the daily-dosed group as the comparison that makes the interval the variable

result.caption: Direction and rank order as reported in the source study, in which spaced schedules largely spared glucose handling while mTORC1 inhibition was retained. Schematic, not measured values.

conclude: Spacing the doses kept glucose handling near the untreated range while mTORC1 inhibition was still there, so the two can come apart in a living animal without changing the molecule.
Schedule is a variable in its own right, alongside dose and chemistry — and it is the one most often left out of the methods sentence.
cannotConclude: That the benefit survives the change. This study measured side-effect endpoints and no lifespan or healthspan outcome, so it shows the harm shrinking rather than the benefit being kept.
That the second complex was untouched on the spaced schedules. What was reported is that no effect on it was detectable under that assay, which is a narrower statement.
nodes.informative: Cheap and load-bearing for the last sub-question, and the step most likely to be over-read. Notice how easily the honest version — harm reduced, benefit not measured — turns into the sentence people actually quote.

interpret.label: It supports my hypothesis
interpret.note: For the wrong-complex reading it supports the practical half: if the cost tracks prolonged exposure, spacing the exposure should reduce it, and it did in these cohorts.

interpret.label: It weakens my hypothesis
interpret.note: It weakens any reading in which the drug's harms follow inevitably from its target engagement, since here the two were separated by a calendar alone.

interpret.label: It is inconclusive for my question
interpret.note: Right for the question as asked. Nothing here touches the residue on mTORC1 outputs; it is about the cost of keeping the drug on.

interpret.label: It introduces an alternative explanation
interpret.note: It introduces a design lesson: an endpoint that was never measured is the easiest thing in the world to read into a result. The benefit endpoint is missing from this study by design.

nodes.opensNote: If a calendar can separate them, the question is whether a molecule can do it more cleanly.

falsify.prompt: What result here would weaken the reading you are holding?

options.label: Spacing the doses changes nothing — the cost tracks the dose, not the exposure
options.note: That would tie the metabolic cost to target engagement itself and leave scheduling as a dead end. It is the result that would push the whole question towards a different molecule.
