options.label: Spaced schedules spare glucose handling while mTORC1 inhibition is kept
options.note: What the source study reports, with the endpoint it actually measured: the harm shrinks. Whether the benefit survives is not in this experiment, and it is the sentence most often read into it.

options.label: Spacing removes the metabolic cost and the target engagement together
options.note: That would make the schedule a blunt dose reduction rather than a separation, which is the alternative reading this design exists to rule out.

options.label: Nothing here would change my mind
options.note: Then the fifteen units are confirming a schedule you have already chosen, and the missing benefit endpoint will still be missing afterwards.

nodes.label: Build a molecule that blocks mTORC1 deeply and leaves the second complex alone
nodes.equipment: A bivalent compound, resistant breast-cancer models, patient-derived xenografts, and then a first-in-human dose-escalation trial. The whole apparatus of drug development, and priced accordingly.
nodes.addresses: Whether depth of block and complex selectivity can be had at the same time

design.model: Human breast-cancer lines and mouse patient-derived xenografts; then dose escalation in advanced solid tumours
design.perturbation: A bi-steric molecule engaging an FKBP12-dependent site and the active site at once
design.readout: Suppression of p-4E-BP1 and the state of Akt Ser473, plus safety and disease control in the trial
design.control: Rapalog-treated and untreated models in the preclinical arm; no randomised comparator in the trial, which is the design's main limit

result.unit: Depth of mTORC1 block against sparing of the second complex
result.caption: Direction and rank order as reported in the source studies, which describe over twenty-five-fold selectivity for mTORC1 over the second complex alongside suppression of the rapamycin-resistant substrate. Schematic, not measured values.

conclude: The two properties are not forced to trade off: a molecule can reach the substrate rapamycin leaves alone and still leave the second complex largely engaged.
The residue identified in cells in 2009 was specific enough to design against, which is what a well-posed mechanistic question eventually buys.
cannotConclude: That sparing the second complex is why the metabolic signal stayed low in the trial. It was open-label and single-arm with no head-to-head comparator, so the low rate sits against historical experience rather than against a control group.
Anything about ageing: these are tumour models and an oncology trial, and the endpoints are tumour endpoints.
nodes.informative: High for the mechanism and deliberately silent on the sub-question left open. It is the step that shows the design problem is soluble, and the step that makes the absence of an ageing readout impossible to miss.

interpret.label: It supports my hypothesis
interpret.note: For partial block, it closes the loop: the residue was real, it was drug-shaped, and a differently shaped drug removes it. For wrong-complex, it supports the practical half — the cost can be engineered away rather than merely rescheduled.

interpret.label: It weakens my hypothesis
interpret.note: For readout-artefact, decisively: a molecule designed against a supposed artefact would have nothing to show, and this one has preclinical and early trial data.

interpret.label: It is inconclusive for my question
interpret.note: Fair for the question this challenge ends on. It shows the chemistry is possible without showing what the chemistry buys where the benefit was claimed.

interpret.label: It introduces an alternative explanation
interpret.note: It introduces a scoping problem instead: the mechanism was read out in one disease area, and the benefit everyone is interested in was measured in another. Nothing joins them yet.

nodes.opensNote: One step remains, and it is the one nobody in this corpus has taken.

falsify.prompt: Before the selective molecule: name the result that would weaken your model.

options.label: Depth and selectivity trade off — reaching 4E-BP1 costs the second complex
options.note: That would make the two properties inseparable and turn the metabolic cost into the price of a deep block. It is the result that would end the selective-inhibitor programme, and it is the one to watch for.

options.label: The molecule suppresses 4E-BP1 and leaves Akt Ser473 largely engaged
options.note: What the source studies report in resistant tumour models and in a single-arm dose-escalation trial. It shows the design problem is soluble; it shows nothing about an ageing endpoint.

options.label: The molecule behaves like a rapalog
options.note: That would say the bivalent design does not deliver what it promises, and the preclinical comparison on this card is the arm that would have shown it.

options.label: Nothing here would change my mind
options.note: Thirty-five units is the second-largest item on the menu. Buying it with no result in mind that would move you is the definition of an expensive habit.

nodes.label: Run a selective molecule against an ageing endpoint
nodes.equipment: Long-lived cohorts of both sexes, a selective compound dosed for most of a lifespan, survival and metabolic endpoints in the same animals. The most equipment on this menu, and part of why nobody in this corpus has it.
nodes.addresses: Whether a block that spares the second complex keeps the lifespan benefit without the metabolic cost. No study in this Atlas corpus reports it: the selective molecules have been read out against tumour endpoints, and the survival data come from rapamycin.

design.model: Genetically heterogeneous mice of both sexes, dosed for most of the lifespan
design.perturbation: A selective mTORC1 inhibitor, against rapamycin and against vehicle
design.readout: Survival, glucose handling and mTORC1 output in the same animals
design.control: A vehicle cohort and a rapamycin cohort at matched target engagement, so the comparison is about selectivity rather than about dose

evidence.basis: No study in this Atlas corpus reports this experiment. What follows is the outcome the model above predicts, written as a prediction and labelled as one. Treat it as a hypothesis to be tested, not as a result to cite.

result.caption: Expected, not observed. These bars are what the teaching model predicts if the benefit tracks mTORC1 and the metabolic cost tracks the second complex. Nothing in the Atlas corpus reports this measurement.

conclude: Only a survival endpoint would turn the mechanistic separation into an answer about the benefit rather than a story about it.
Running rapamycin alongside at matched target engagement is what would make the comparison readable, and it is the arm most likely to be cut for cost.
cannotConclude: Anything at all, until it is done. Reading a predicted pattern as evidence is the specific error this challenge is built to make visible.
Sex is not a nuisance variable here: the reported effects on lifespan differ between males and females, so a single-sex cohort would answer a narrower question than the one asked.
nodes.informative: The highest in principle, and a gap in this corpus rather than a line in it. Choosing it costs 40 units and returns a prediction — which is a fair picture of what committing to an unpublished experiment feels like from the inside.

interpret.label: It supports my hypothesis
interpret.note: A prediction cannot support a hypothesis; it is generated by one. If this felt like support while you were reading it, that reflex is what the labelling is here to interrupt.

interpret.label: It weakens my hypothesis
interpret.note: Also not something a prediction can do. What it can do is tell you which hypothesis you would give up if the experiment came out the other way, which is worth writing down before it runs.

interpret.label: It is inconclusive for my question
interpret.note: Correct, and the useful follow-up is: what would you have to see here to change your mind? Naming that in advance is most of what makes an experiment worth its budget.

interpret.label: It introduces an alternative explanation
interpret.note: It introduces a design problem rather than an explanation: lifelong dosing, two sexes and matched engagement are three expensive requirements, and dropping any one of them changes what the survival curve would mean.

rules.note: You closed the investigation without spending anything. That is a legitimate move only if you had already decided the menu could not move the question — and if so, the reasoning for that belongs in the final step.

The second antibody is where this challenge starts paying. Fifteen units on a lysate you already had turned ‘the drug works’ into ‘the drug works unevenly’, which is the observation everything else here explains or fails to explain.

You bought the famous band and stopped. Every hypothesis on your list predicted it, so ten units went on shared background — and the cheapest follow-up on the menu, on the same lysates, was the one that would have shown the split.

The chemistry comparison did the discriminating work. It is the one place where the partial-block reading and the readout-artefact reading expect different things, and the result went against the second.

You never put a second chemistry next to the first. Without one, a surviving signal is compatible with a partial block, with an artefact of the readout, and with the network answering back — which is why the question can still feel open at the end.

Chemistry and feedback measured rather than argued about. This pair is the strongest route through the menu for the question as posed: one says the residue is drug-shaped, the other says how much of the cell moved while you were looking.

You found the time-dependent arm and left the cheapest follow-up unbought. Fifteen units would have shown whether the cost tracks exposure closely enough for a calendar to separate it — which is the part of this story with consequences outside the dish.

The full route through the second axis: the cost appears with prolonged exposure, shrinks when the schedule is spaced, and can be engineered out with a differently shaped molecule. Notice what all three still lack — a benefit endpoint.

You bought the schedule comparison without the step that says why the schedule should matter. The result stands on its own, but the reason it is interesting — that the cost tracks prolonged exposure — is the 30-unit step you skipped.

Forty units, the largest single item, bought a prediction rather than a result, and the card said so before you paid. That makes it a decision rather than a trap, and it is roughly what committing to an unpublished experiment costs.

Everything you ran describes the unevenness, and nothing you ran explains it. Three consistent descriptions of the same phenomenon are not evidence about its cause — the ruler was the missing 25 units.

model.title: The model you are arguing with
model.caption: Two chemistries on the left, one kinase in the middle, and three outputs on the right. The drug switch chooses nothing, rapamycin or an active-site inhibitor; the clock switch chooses acute or prolonged exposure. Nodes and arrows come from the Atlas pathway model, so this teaching diagram cannot drift away from the scientific one.

controls.label: Drug
options: none
rapamycin
active-site

controls.label: Exposure
options: acute
prolonged

none|acute.readout: p-S6K1 high  ·  p-4E-BP1 high  ·  autophagy held down  ·  Akt Ser473 phosphorylated
none|acute.note: The reference state. Note what an active kinase does to two of the arrows: phosphorylated 4E-BP1 lets go of eIF4E, and phosphorylated ULK1 cannot be switched on, so a growing cell builds protein and keeps recycling down. Both of those are brakes being held off rather than accelerators being pressed.

none|prolonged.readout: p-S6K1 high  ·  p-4E-BP1 high  ·  autophagy held down  ·  Akt Ser473 phosphorylated
none|prolonged.note: With no drug on, the clock changes nothing. The state is here so you can hold one switch still while you move the other — the comparison that makes a time-dependent effect visible at all.

rapamycin|acute.readout: p-S6K1 low  ·  p-4E-BP1 largely retained  ·  autophagy partly released  ·  Akt Ser473 phosphorylated
rapamycin|acute.note: Sit with this one; it is the state a decade of papers reported as ‘mTORC1 off’. The S6K1 arm is gone, and the kinase is still phosphorylating 4E-BP1, so protein is still being built. IRS-1 lights up because the brake on it went with S6K1 — the treated cell has a livelier insulin arm than the untreated one.

rapamycin|prolonged.readout: p-S6K1 low  ·  p-4E-BP1 largely retained  ·  Akt Ser473 lost in the sensitive lines  ·  glucose handling disturbed in mice
rapamycin|prolonged.note: Same drug, same dose, different answer to the question ‘what does it block?’. New mTORC2 stops being assembled, Akt loses its second phosphate, and in mice the metabolic cost appears. The Atlas draws this arrow dashed and grades it contested, because it is absent acutely and varies between cell lines.

active-site|acute.readout: p-S6K1 low  ·  p-4E-BP1 low  ·  cap-dependent translation down  ·  autophagy induced  ·  Akt Ser473 low
active-site|acute.note: Occupying the active site rather than obstructing the doorway gives a different pattern from the first click: 4E-BP1 stays unphosphorylated, keeps hold of eIF4E, and protein synthesis goes with it. The same site sits in both complexes, so the second complex goes down too — at once, not after days.

active-site|prolonged.readout: p-S6K1 low  ·  p-4E-BP1 low  ·  cap-dependent translation down  ·  autophagy induced  ·  Akt Ser473 low
active-site|prolonged.note: Here the clock is the uninteresting switch. This chemistry hits both complexes from the first minutes, so there is no second phase to wait for — which is the contrast that makes the time axis a real finding for the other drug rather than a detail of dosing.

break.prompt: Set the drug to rapamycin and the clock to acute. Two of the three output arms are in the model. Which readout would report the pathway as switched off, and which would report it still running?
options: p-S6K1 would report it off, and p-4E-BP1 would report output continuing
Both readouts would report it off
Both readouts would report output continuing
The model cannot represent this
break.explain: The two arms come apart in this state, and which one you blot for decides what you would write in the abstract. That is why a decade of papers using p-S6K1 as the readout of mTORC1 activity over-reported how much of the kinase rapamycin was switching off.

break.prompt: Keep the drug at rapamycin and move the clock from acute to prolonged. A part of the diagram lights up that was dark before. What does that do to the sentence ‘rapamycin is an mTORC1 inhibitor’?
options: Nothing — the drug has one target and the clock is a detail of dosing
The second complex joins the picture, so the target list depends on how long the drug has been on
mTORC1 becomes fully blocked once the exposure is long enough
The model cannot represent this
break.explain: The sentence is not wrong so much as unfinished: it needs a duration attached. An acute experiment and a chronic one are asking different questions of the same molecule, and much of the disagreement in this literature is two groups reporting honestly from either side of that clock.

break.prompt: Three states in this model give a low p-S6K1 and differ in almost everything else. What follows for a paper that reports only that band?
options: Nothing — p-S6K1 is the standard readout of mTORC1 activity
A low p-S6K1 does not say which chemistry or which exposure produced it, so the design needs a second substrate or a second time point
p-S6K1 should be replaced by p-4E-BP1 in every design
The model is wrong, because one readout should identify one cause
break.explain: A readout earns its place in proportion to how differently the candidate explanations predict it. This one is a fine measure of the S6K1 arm and a poor discriminator between the four explanations you are about to choose from, because three quite different states of the cell collapse onto the same band.

hypotheses.prompt: Commit to a working hypothesis before you spend anything. It is meant to be revised later — that is what the second half of this challenge is for.

options.label: The block is partial by construction
options.note: The drug obstructs the doorway to the kinase rather than filling its catalytic pocket, so substrates that need deep, sustained access lose out and others carry on. It predicts that a chemistry which does occupy the site reaches further, and that the split between outputs is reproducible rather than noise. Its weak point: obstruction and network feedback predict the same blot in a single-time-point experiment.

options.label: The incompleteness is in the readout, not the drug
options.note: On this reading mTORC1 really is switched off and the persisting signal is an artefact of which band gets blotted, of antibody sensitivity, or of a phosphosite that another kinase also touches. It predicts that a wider substrate panel, or a functional readout instead of a phosphosite, makes the residue disappear. It is the hypothesis most worth holding early and the easiest to hold too long.

options.label: The network answers back
options.note: Block the kinase and the loops around it re-set: S6K1 stops repressing IRS-1, upstream receptor signalling picks up, and the cell you measure is no longer the untreated cell with one arrow cut. It predicts that the residue grows over time rather than staying flat, and that the arm above the kinase moves in the same lysates. It has to explain why a deeper chemistry, which relieves the same feedback, still gives a deeper block.

options.label: The interesting part is the complex the drug was not supposed to touch
options.note: Here the incompleteness on mTORC1 is the less consequential half of the story, and what matters is that prolonged exposure reaches the second complex, taking the arm to Akt with it. It predicts that the drug's effects at day ten are not the drug's effects at minute ten. Its weak point as an answer to the question asked: it explains the side effects better than it explains the residue.

revise.prompt: Your working hypothesis, after the evidence you bought
revise.note: Changing your mind here is the expected outcome, not a failure state. A first hypothesis that survives every experiment untouched usually means the experiments were not discriminating.

feedback.partial-block: The drug comparison is the strongest support available in this corpus for this reading, and it comes with a scope: what you have is a difference between two chemistries on a panel of substrates in cells. Holding it well means saying which substrates, at which dose, and keeping the feedback arm in view as a second contributor rather than a rival.
feedback.readout-artefact: Hard to hold once a second chemistry is in the experiment, because the residue moves when the drug changes and the antibody does not. Worth keeping a narrow version of it: a phosphosite is still a proxy, and the functional readouts in this challenge behave more like the phosphosites than most people expect.
feedback.feedback: Well supported as a real contributor and hard to hold as the whole answer: relief of the upstream brake happens under either chemistry, so it cannot by itself explain why one of them reaches further. The version that survives is a joint one, where obstruction sets the floor and feedback decides how fast the signal creeps back up.
feedback.wrong-complex: Right about the most consequential part of the drug's behaviour and slightly off the question as posed. The second-complex arm is where the metabolic cost lives and where the schedule and the selective molecule earn their place — but the residue on 4E-BP1 sits inside mTORC1 signalling and needs the chemistry comparison rather than the time axis.

compare.whatTheyTested: What an inhibitor that occupies the active site would reveal about the one everybody was already using — measured as phosphorylation of both mTORC1 substrates, as cap-dependent translation, and as autophagy induction, in matched cultures side by side.
whatItAnswered: Rapamycin leaves a class of mTORC1 outputs largely running, 4E-BP1 phosphorylation among them.
Autophagy sits in that class too, so the drug's best-known effect is also its partial one.
The residue is a property of the chemistry rather than a limit of the kinase, since a different chemistry reaches further.
whatItDidNot: It did not read the second complex over days, so the time axis of this challenge is outside its design.
The active-site compound is not complex-selective, so it cannot say which complex each part of the deeper effect came from.
It is cell-line pharmacology: how much of the residue matters in any particular tissue or tumour is not something this design measures.
compare.howToRead: The published experiment is not the perfect version of your design, and it was never meant to be. It is a real design with its own controls, its own scope and its own limits — and reading it that way rather than as a verdict is the skill this step is for. Compare it with what you chose: which of your unspent steps would you now run alongside it?

options: A result came out differently from what I predicted
A result was what I expected but did not separate the hypotheses
A limitation or a confounder made me re-read a result I had already accepted
Nothing changed; I ended where I started

reflection.prompt: Which evidence mattered most to your final position?
options: The second antibody on the same lysates
The head-to-head comparison of two chemistries
The time axis, and what prolonged exposure reached
The absence of the experiment I most wanted to run

nextQuestion.text: The list above is where a next experiment would go. Pick the one you would defend in front of someone holding the budget — not the most interesting one, the one that would change what the field can say.
nextQuestion.prompt: You have one more opportunity and a limited budget. What would you do next?

options.label: Run a second-complex-sparing molecule against a survival endpoint, with rapamycin alongside at matched target engagement
options.note: The direct attack on the gap, and the most expensive option on any realistic menu. Budget both sexes and the rapamycin arm from the start: without the comparator the survival curve cannot separate selectivity from dose, and without both sexes it answers a narrower question than the one asked.

options.label: Apportion the two routes to disturbed glucose handling in one set of animals
options.note: Cheaper and badly needed. Loss of the second complex and relief of the S6K1-to-IRS-1 brake have never been weighed against each other in the same experiment, and the answer would tell you whether a selective molecule can spare the metabolic cost or only part of it.

options.label: Map the residue across a wide substrate panel and a dose-response, in more than one cell type
options.note: The unglamorous option that would firm up the foundation. Much of what we call rapamycin-resistant output rests on a handful of substrates in a handful of lines; knowing which substrates behave that way, and how reproducibly, would sharpen every design downstream.

options.label: Read the second-complex effect across lines, doses and durations to find where it actually appears
options.note: Follows the most contested edge in this story rather than the original question. The Atlas grades it contested because sensitivity varies; a systematic map would turn a caveat into a rule of thumb, which is worth more than it sounds for anyone choosing a schedule.

The output route, where the substrates this challenge argues about do their work.

answer.short: On the evidence in this Atlas: because of how it inhibits, and then, after long enough, because of where it ends up. The drug obstructs the doorway to the kinase rather than filling its catalytic pocket, so some substrates keep their access — and prolonged exposure adds a second target that acute exposure leaves alone.

observation.text: Rapamycin binds FKBP12 and the pair docks on a site adjacent to the kinase's active site rather than in it.
Treatment takes p-S6K1 down within minutes, and that band became the standard readout of mTORC1 activity.
Against an active-site inhibitor as a ruler, rapamycin leaves 4E-BP1 phosphorylation largely in place and induces autophagy only partly.
Inhibiting mTORC1 relieves feedback onto receptor signalling, and Akt phosphorylation can rise rather than fall.
Prolonged exposure reduces assembly of the second complex in sensitive lines, and the same loss appears in mouse liver alongside disturbed glucose handling.
Spacing the doses in mice largely spared glucose handling while mTORC1 inhibition was retained; side-effect endpoints only, with no benefit endpoint measured.
A bi-steric molecule suppresses the rapamycin-resistant substrate while sparing the second complex, in resistant tumour models and in a single-arm dose-escalation trial.

interpretation: Read together, these support a two-axis picture rather than a single number for potency. Chemistry decides the depth of the block on mTORC1 outputs: obstruction of the substrate channel leaves some substrates reachable, and occupying the active site does not. Duration decides its breadth: acutely one complex, after prolonged exposure often both. Most apparent disagreements about ‘how much rapamycin inhibits mTOR’ turn out to be two groups reporting from different corners of those two axes.

The network's reply is a real third contributor and not a rival to the first. Relieving the brake on the arm above the kinase happens under either chemistry, so it cannot be why one reaches further — but it does mean a treated cell is not an untreated cell with one arrow cut, and it sets how fast a partly blocked signal creeps back.

What the drug does, then, is not to turn mTORC1 output down by a fixed fraction but to reshape which outputs stay on. That reshaping is a plausible reason the same molecule can extend lifespan in mice while performing modestly as a single agent against many tumours, and it is why ‘rapamycin induces autophagy’ needs the dose, the cell type and the readout attached before it is a claim.
stillOpen: No study in this corpus joins a second-complex-sparing molecule to an ageing endpoint. The selective compounds were read out against tumour endpoints; the survival data come from rapamycin. That join is the 40-unit item on your menu that returns a prediction, and it is the same gap the Atlas records as H2.

Two routes lead from mTORC1 inhibition to disturbed glucose handling — loss of the second complex, and relief of the S6K1-to-IRS-1 brake — and their relative contribution in people has not been apportioned. The Atlas's own edge on that feedback arm records the missing apportionment rather than papering over it.

Whether prolonged exposure reaches the second complex in a given cell depends on line, dose and duration, and what the spaced-schedule study reports is that no effect on it was detectable under its assay. ‘Not detected here’ and ‘not happening’ are different claims, and the difference matters for anyone choosing a schedule.

hypothesisVerdicts.partial-block: The reading the evidence best supports for the question as asked, once it is stated with its scope: steric obstruction rather than occupancy, measured across a substrate panel in cells, with the chemistry comparison as the load-bearing result. It got sharper rather than failing — the qualified version names substrates and a mechanism instead of a potency.
hypothesisVerdicts.readout-artefact: Does not survive the chemistry comparison. The residue moves when the molecule changes while the antibodies stay the same, and it shows up on a functional readout as well as on phosphosites. A narrow version is still worth keeping: a phosphosite is a proxy, and this challenge is partly about how much weight one band carries.
hypothesisVerdicts.feedback: Right about a real contributor, wrong as the whole answer. Relief of the upstream brake is measured, and it happens under either chemistry, so it cannot explain why one reaches further. The version that survives is joint: obstruction sets the floor, feedback sets how quickly the signal comes back.
hypothesisVerdicts.wrong-complex: Half-right in a way worth naming precisely. The second-complex arm is where the metabolic cost lives, and it is the half with consequences outside the dish — but it is time-dependent, graded contested, and silent about the residue on 4E-BP1, which sits inside mTORC1 signalling.
